claims.text: Brittle behavior in initially single-phase HEAs emerges from stress-induced short-range chemical ordering localized at grain boundaries.
Pre-existing impurity segregation is not the cause of the proposed brittle behavior.
Mechanical loading activates atomic rearrangements at grain boundaries that foster local chemical ordering.
Cyclic loading or low-temperature loading particularly promotes the proposed grain-boundary ordering.
Localized grain-boundary ordering reduces grain-boundary cohesive energy or strength.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion caused by SRO triggers brittle intergranular fracture.
Conventional-alloy grain-boundary embrittlement instead arises from slow thermally driven impurity segregation or brittle secondary precipitate formation.
The initial HEA is a single-phase, chemically disordered solid solution.
The initial HEA has uniformly high toughness.
Mechanically loaded specimens will exhibit a measurable increase in grain-boundary SRO relative to undeformed controls.
The proposed increase in grain-boundary SRO can be detected by atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM.
Mechanically loaded specimens will have lower fracture toughness or tensile ductility than the as-processed baseline.
Mechanical loading will shift fracture behavior from ductile failure toward intergranular brittle failure.
Loading must be sufficiently severe to trigger atomistic rearrangements for the proposed mechanism to operate.
Insufficient atomic mobility at very low temperature can prevent significant ordering and limit the mechanism.
High-cycle fatigue or high-strain-rate loading are candidate conditions capable of triggering the proposed rearrangements.
